feedback.nudge: Two numbers: how many events there are, and what each one is worth. Multiply. The bound asks for nothing else — no inclusion-exclusion, no independence.

explanation:
## The computation

$A_i$ specifies five particular tosses and says nothing about the rest, so

$$\P(A_i) = \Bigl(\tfrac12\Bigr)^{5} = \tfrac1{32}.$$

A run of five can start at position $1, 2, \dots, 16$, so there are sixteen events and

$$\P\Bigl(\bigcup_{i=1}^{16} A_i\Bigr) \;\le\; \sum_{i=1}^{16} \P(A_i) \;=\; \frac{16}{32} \;=\; \frac12 .$$

## What makes the bound worth having

Nothing about the $A_i$ was used except their individual probabilities. They are not disjoint — $A_1 \cap A_2$ is the event that tosses 1 to 6 are all heads, with probability $1/64$ — and they are not independent. Inclusion–exclusion would need all $2^{16}$ intersections.

The union bound is the fact that none of that matters when you only want an upper bound. It is countable subadditivity, it follows from the axioms in two lines with indicators, and it is probably the single most used inequality in probability.

## How good is it here?

The true probability of a run of five heads in twenty fair tosses is about $0.25$. So the bound of $0.5$ is out by a factor of two — loose, and still in the right region.

The bound degrades exactly when the events overlap a lot or when there are many of them. Ask the same question for a run of **three** heads in twenty tosses: eighteen events of probability $1/8$ each gives a bound of $18/8 = 2.25$, which is true and says nothing at all. A bound above 1 is the signal that the events are overlapping too much for this tool.

## Where it is sharp

The union bound is an equality exactly when the events are disjoint. More usefully, it is *nearly* sharp when the events are rare and barely overlap — which is why it is the workhorse of the probabilistic method: to prove that something with no bad property exists, show that the sum of the probabilities of the bad events is below 1.
